grades.quote: One situation is a system call, when a user program executes the ecall instruction to ask the kernel to do something for it.
grades.reason: Names the RISC-V ecall instruction as how a user program asks the kernel for a service. It also explains that this forces a transfer of control to kernel handler code.

grades.quote: The ecall instruction traps from user space into the kernel and causes uservec, usertrap, and then syscall to execute.
grades.reason: Shows that ecall traps from user space into the kernel and runs the handler chain (uservec, usertrap, syscall). It also shows the syscall number being passed in a7.

grades.quote: the execution of the SYSCALL instruction will trigger the system call exception immediately.
grades.reason: Identifies the LoongArch SYSCALL instruction as the one that triggers the system call exception. The passage also says a triggered exception switches control flow to the handler entry.

grades.quote: The trap is a synchronous exception that is an explicit call to the execution environment requesting an action on behalf of software inside the execution environment. An example is a system call.
grades.reason: Describes the RISC-V concept of a requested trap, with a system call as an example. It does not name the instruction that performs it, so it only gives limited auxiliary context.
